# Opening: Christ had no biological father

**Definition.** "Biological father" means a male parent who supplies the seed of conception. The question is whether any man did so for Christ. [L4, resting on Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:20, both exhibited below]

## 1. The genealogy stops begetting at Joseph

[L1] Matthew 1:2-15 repeats "begat" through the whole line. Matthew 1:16 then reads: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

[L2] The verb in verses 2-16 is ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat"), active voice, with a man as subject. In verse 16 the pattern breaks. The text reads ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη (ex hēs egennēthē, "out of whom was born"). The relative pronoun ἧς (hēs, "whom") is feminine singular, so it can refer only to Mary. The verb is passive. Joseph is called ἄνδρα (andra, "husband, man"), not the one who begat.

[L3] Within the same chapter the writer uses "begat" thirty-nine times for the male line. He drops it exactly at Joseph. Christ is "born of" Mary, not "begotten by" Joseph.

## 2. The conception is attributed to the Holy Ghost

[L1] Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

[L2] The phrase is ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Spirit holy"). The preposition ἐκ (ek, "out of") marks source. The participle γεννηθὲν (gennēthen, "that which was begotten/conceived") is neuter, "that which," and it is located ἐν αὐτῇ (en autē, "in her"). The source is named as the Spirit, and the place is her womb.

[L3] Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee." The verbs are ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai, "will come upon") and ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "will overshadow"). Luke names the same agent as Matthew. "Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." The "therefore" (διό, dio, "for which reason") makes the Spirit's action the cause of his being called Son of God. Matthew 1:18 also fixes the timing: "before they came together."

## 3. Mary was a virgin and said so

[L1] Luke 1:27: "to a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph." Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" Matthew 1:25: Joseph "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son."

[L2] In Luke 1:27 the word is παρθένον (parthenon, "virgin"). In Luke 1:34 the phrase is ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (andra ou ginōskō, "a man I do not know"). The verb γινώσκω (ginōskō, "to know") carries the sexual sense, as in Genesis 4:1 LXX. In Matthew 1:25 the imperfect ἐγίνωσκεν (eginōsken, "was knowing") with ἕως οὗ (heōs hou, "until which") puts the birth at the point where the abstention ended.

[L3] Luke 1:34 asks how a conception could happen without a man, and verse 35 answers with the Spirit, not with a man. The question and the answer fit together.

## 4. Joseph's fatherhood is only reputed

[L1] Luke 3:23: "Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."

[L2] ὡς ἐνομίζετο (hōs enomizeto, "as was being reckoned/supposed") describes opinion, not fact. The verb νομίζω (nomizō, "to think, to suppose") is used for a belief that may be mistaken, as in Acts 16:27.

[L3] Matthew 1:19-20 shows Joseph "minded to put her away privily." The angel tells him, "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife." Joseph himself had not fathered the conception. Luke 2:48-49 has Mary say "thy father and I have sought thee." The child answers, "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" (ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου, en tois tou patros mou, "in the things of my Father"). He corrects the title. The crowd's "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?" (John 6:42) reports what the crowd supposed, not what the text asserts.

## 5. Scripture's pattern: her seed, a body prepared

[L1] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed." Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman." Hebrews 10:5: "a body hast thou prepared me."

[L2] In Genesis 3:15 the word is זַרְעָהּ (zarʿāh, "her seed"). Seed is ordinarily reckoned to the man, so this phrasing is distinctive. In Galatians 4:4 the phrase is γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come to be out of a woman"). Only the woman is named as source. In Hebrews 10:5 the verb is κατηρτίσω (katērtisō, "you fitted, prepared"), which points to a body furnished by God.

[L3] Isaiah 7:14, "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son," is cited in Matthew 1:22-23 as fulfilled. The Hebrew הָעַלְמָה (hāʿalmāh, "the young woman, the virgin") is used of Rebekah in Genesis 24:43, whom Genesis 24:16 describes as a virgin "neither had any man known her." Matthew renders it with παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin").

## Anticipated objection: "seed of David"

[L1] Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." Luke 1:32: "the throne of his father David."

[L2] Paul's phrase is κατὰ σάρκα (kata sarka, "according to flesh"), and it names descent from David without naming a father. "Father David" is an ancestral title, as in Luke 1:73 "our father Abraham."

[L3] Luke 3:23-31 runs the line through Nathan, David's son. Matthew 1:11-12 runs Joseph's line through Jechonias, of whom Jeremiah 22:30 says "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David." A biological descent from Joseph through that line would carry that bar. [L4, resting on Jeremiah 22:30 and Matthew 1:11-12]

Nor is God the Father a "biological father." John 4:24 says "God is a Spirit," and Luke 24:39 says "a spirit hath not flesh and bones." The Spirit's action in Luke 1:35 is the cause of the conception, not a male supplying seed.

## DECLARED CHAIN -- the links your case stands on

1. Matthew 1:16 breaks the "begat" pattern of verses 2-15 at Joseph and traces the birth to Mary alone. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:16; [L2] ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη (ex hēs egennēthē, "out of whom was born"), feminine relative pronoun, passive verb, against active ἐγέννησεν (egennēsen, "begat"); [L3] the thirty-nine uses of "begat" in Matthew 1:2-15.
2. The conception in Mary is attributed to the Holy Ghost, before Joseph and Mary came together. Footing: [L1] Matthew 1:18, 20; [L2] ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Spirit holy"), ἐν αὐτῇ (en autē, "in her"); [L3] Luke 1:35, ἐπελεύσεται and ἐπισκιάσει ("come upon," "overshadow"), with διό (dio, "therefore").
3. Mary was a virgin and no man had known her. Footing: [L1] Luke 1:27, 34 and Matthew 1:25; [L2] παρθένον (parthenon, "virgin"), ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (andra ou ginōskō, "a man I do not know"), ἐγίνωσκεν (eginōsken, "was knowing"); [L3] Genesis 24:16, 43 and Isaiah 7:14 as cited in Matthew 1:22-23.
4. Joseph was the reputed father only. Footing: [L1] Luke 3:23, Matthew 1:19-20; [L2] ὡς ἐνομίζετο (hōs enomizeto, "as was supposed"); [L3] Luke 2:48-49 (the child's "my Father's business") and John 6:42 (the crowd's report).
5. The pattern of "her seed" and "made of a woman" gives Mary alone as the human source, and David's seed is traced through her line. Footing: [L1] Genesis 3:15, Galatians 4:4, Romans 1:3, Hebrews 10:5; [L2] זַרְעָהּ (zarʿāh, "her seed"), γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos, "come to be out of a woman"), κατηρτίσω (katērtisō, "you prepared"); [L3] Luke 3:31 with Matthew 1:11-12 and Jeremiah 22:30.
6. Christ had no biological father. He was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, and Joseph was his father only by supposition and legal standing. Footing: links 1-5, resting on [L1] Matthew 1:16-25 and Luke 1:34-35, [L2] ἐκ πνεύματος ἁγίου (ek pneumatos hagiou, "out of Spirit holy") with ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (andra ou ginōskō, "a man I do not know"), and [L3] Galatians 4:4 and Isaiah 7:14.

# Reply: the chain breaks at every link where the text names a man

The definition is agreed: a biological father is a male parent who supplies the seed of conception. So the only question is whether the text names a man as the source of that seed. It names one, in plain words, and the chain never quotes those words.

---

## Against D1 — Matthew 1:16

Your [L2] observation is correct and I grant the morphology: ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη (ex hēs egennēthē, "out of whom was born") is passive, and the feminine pronoun points to Mary. What the verse does *not* say is your conclusion. "Of whom was born" states the birth from the mother; it does not state that the father supplied nothing. The same verse names him: "Jacob begat Joseph **the husband of Mary**" [L1]. Matthew 1:19 names him again, "Joseph her husband"; 1:20, "Mary thy wife." A husband is named in the very row you call the pattern-break.

Two more problems [L1-L2-L3]:

1. **The passive cannot bear the weight.** Matthew 1:16 narrates the birth, not the begetting; no verb of knowledge or denial occurs in it [L1; L2: egennēthē carries no negation]. A verse that stops short of naming the father is not a verse that says he was absent — that step is yours [L4].
2. **If Joseph supplies no seed, your own genealogy is empty.** The promise requires flesh seed out of a man's body: "I will set up thy seed after thee, **which shall proceed out of thy bowels**" (2 Samuel 7:12) [L1]; "of the fruit of his loins, **according to the flesh**, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne" (Acts 2:30) [L1]; "it is evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda" (Hebrews 7:14) [L1]. Reading Matthew 1:2-16 as thirty-nine *biological* begets and one non-biological close gives you a line with no flesh seed in it at exactly the point where the flesh is required. And the reckoning is by the father's house in any case: "by the house of their fathers... every male by their polls" (Numbers 1:2), "declared their pedigrees... by the house of their fathers" (1:18) [L1, L3].

---

## Against D2 — "of the Holy Ghost"

Matthew 1:18, 20 are quoted as written and stand as written. But the inference that this names the *begetter* is not in the row.

- **ek + God/Spirit names origin, not paternity**, across the New Testament: "born of God" (John 1:13; 1 John 3:9; 5:1), "is of God" (1 John 4:7) — every one spiritual/covenant, none biological [L1-L3].
- **The flesh-marker is absent.** Where Paul means biological flesh he says it: ἐκ σπέρματος Δαυὶδ **κατὰ σάρκα** (ek spermatos David kata sarka, "of the seed of David according to flesh," Romans 1:3) [L2]. Matthew 1:20 has no kata sarka attached to the Spirit phrase. You are reading a paternity into a construction the canon uses for covenant origin.
- **Luke 1:35's verbs never denote begetting.** ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai, "come upon") is the word of Acts 1:8, "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you," of the apostles — anointing and power [L1-L2-L3]; ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "overshadow") is the transfiguration cloud (Luke 9:34) and Peter's healing shadow (Acts 5:15) [L1-L2-L3]. Not one row of either word names conception by a male agency.
- **Your "therefore" runs the wrong way.** Luke 1:32 gives the throne first: "the Lord God shall give unto him **the throne of his father David**" [L1]. Then v.34 asks the question, then v.35 answers and the Sonship is a *title*: "shall be **called** the Son of God" [L1]. The covenant title runs on David's covenant: "I have chosen him to be my son" — said to David **about Solomon**, whom David begat (1 Chronicles 28:6) [L1-L3].
- **The angel's sentence commissions Joseph as father:** "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife... **thou shalt call his name JESUS**" (Matthew 1:20-21), and he does: "he called his name JESUS" (1:25) [L1]. The naming is the father's act.

---

## Against D3 — the virgin and the timing rows

Mary's virginity at the annunciation is granted; the verse never says the state was permanent.

- Luke 1:34: ἄνδρα οὐ γινώσκω (andra ou ginōskō, "a man I know not") is **present indicative** — her state when the angel spoke. A permanent vow would take οὐ μή with the aorist subjunctive; the text does not [L1-L2].
- Matthew 1:18 "before they came together, she was found with child" **dates the finding**, not the act; συνέρχομαι (synerchomai) names married union in Paul — "come together again" (1 Corinthians 7:5) [L1-L2-L3]. Matthew tells you what "came together" means by what follows: "took unto him his wife" (1:24).
- Matthew 1:25: "knew her not **till** she had brought forth her **firstborn** son" (Luke 2:7) [L1]. ἕως οὗ (heōs hou, "until which") bounds the abstinence to the pregnancy; "firstborn" names an order among children — "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, the brother of James...?" and "his sisters, are they not all with us?" (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55-56) [L1-L3]. A permanent abstinence cannot produce a firstborn with brothers and sisters named in the text.
- Your Isaiah 7:14 line: the Hebrew is הָעַלְמָה (hā'almāh, "the young woman"), not בְּתוּלָה (bethulah, "the virgin") [L2] — and your own example proves the word carries the meaning you add: if 'almah meant "virgin," Genesis 24:43 would not need 24:16's gloss "neither had any man known her." The KJV's 1611 margin at Isaiah 7:14 reads "or, thou, O virgin, shalt call."

---

## Against D4 — "reputed father only"

This link sets one parenthesis against four registers of the text's own narration:

- Mary's own mouth: "**thy father** and I have sought thee sorrowing" (Luke 2:48) — said to Jesus, by the woman who received the annunciation [L1].
- The narrator: "the parents brought in the child Jesus" (Luke 2:27); "his parents went to Jerusalem" (2:41); "Joseph and his mother" (2:33, 43) [L1].
- The town: "Is not this **Joseph's son**?" (Luke 4:22); "Jesus, the son of Joseph, **whose father and mother we know**" (John 6:42) [L1].
- A disciple: "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45) [L1].
- The angel: "Joseph, **thou son of David**" (Matthew 1:20) [L1].

On the verb: ὡς ἐνομίζετο (hōs enomizeto, "as was supposed") is the same form as Acts 16:13 "where prayer **was wont** to be made" [L2] — a reckoning word that carries no verdict of its own; each context decides. And Luke 2:49 is not a correction of Joseph: the boy answers about his Father's business in the temple, and the same gospel still says "Joseph and his mother" two verses later (2:43) [L1]. Your John 6:42 move also proves too much: on that rule, "whose father **and mother** we know" cancels the mother as well.

---

## Against D5 — "her seed," "made of a woman," "through her line"

- **"Her seed" (Genesis 3:15) is not a Davidic route.** Seed predicated of a woman in the offspring sense occurs four times (Genesis 3:15; 16:10 of Hagar; 24:60 of Rebekah; Isaiah 54:3 of Zion) — none of them Davidic, and the standard text still counts the seed through the man's house (Numbers 1:2) [L1-L2-L3].
- **"Made of a woman" is the mortality idiom, not a father-denial.** Galatians 4:4 sits beside Job 14:1 "man that is born of a woman is of few days"; 15:14; 25:4; and Matthew 11:11 of John the Baptist — **whose father is named** (Luke 1:13, 67) [L1-L3]. If the phrase excluded a father, John had none. It does not say "and no man."
- **"A body hast thou prepared me" (Hebrews 10:5)** is not a seedless body; Hebrews 2:16 says he "took on him the seed of Abraham" and Hebrews 7:14 "sprang out of Juda" [L1].
- **"Through her line" is the import that carries your flesh claim — and it exhibits no name.** The text gives Mary no lineage: Luke 1:5 names Elisabeth "of the daughters of Aaron," and 1:36 calls her Mary's kinswoman; Luke 3:23 reads "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was [the son] of Heli" — **no female name anywhere in the register** [L1]. "Mary's genealogy" is not in the record.
- **Your Jeremiah 22:30 bar is an inference on an inference.** The curse reads "a man that shall not prosper **in his days**... ruling any more **in Judah**" [L1]; Jeremiah 18:7-8 gives the rule for a pronounced sentence; and the signet plucked at 22:24 is set again on "Zerubbabel... the son of Shealtiel" (Haggai 2:23), who governs Judah (Haggai 1:1; Ezra 3:2) [L1-L3]. Matthew 1:12 says "Jechonias begat Salathiel"; Luke 3:27 says "Salathiel, which was the son of Neri" — whether these are the same men the text never states [L1]. And the New Testament never once cites that curse against Christ. Note the fork you have built yourself: you need Matthew's line to be *biological* for the curse to bar it, and *non-biological* for the virgin birth. It cannot be both.

---

## Against D6 — the keystone

The keystone states what no verse states. Not Matthew 1:16 (which names the husband), not Matthew 1:18 (which dates a finding), not Luke 1:34 (which is present tense), not Luke 1:35 (whose verbs are anointing and presence), not Galatians 4:4 (which is the mortality idiom). Where the text does speak to begetting, it says: "Adam **knew** Eve his wife; and she conceived" (Genesis 4:1) [L1] — the canon's stated means.

So, on two exhibited footings — [L1] the husband rows ("Joseph her husband," Matthew 1:19; "Mary thy wife," 1:20; "his neighbour's wife," Deuteronomy 22:24, the law's word for a betrothed woman; "knew her not **till**," 1:25) and [L3] the seed rows ("proceed out of thy bowels," 2 Samuel 7:12; "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh," Acts 2:30; "made of the seed of David according to the flesh," Romans 1:3; "evident that our Lord sprang out of Juda," Hebrews 7:14) — the inference is: **Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal, and the child is of his loins** [L4]. Every timing row you press is quoted as written and read inside that chain; none of them says "no man," and the abstinence they state is bounded to the pregnancy by "till."

Joseph, then, is the biological father the question asks for: named by Mary as "thy father," named by the narrator as husband, named by the angel as "son of David," the one who names the child, of "the house and lineage of David" (Luke 2:4) [L1]. To say otherwise, the text would have to say so. It never does.

---

Christ is 'born of' Mary, not 'begotten by' Joseph." | Matthew 1:16 "Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary"; 1:19 "Joseph her husband"; Acts 2:30 "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh." # Round 2: the chain holds. The challenger's own grants close it.

Under Isaiah 28:10 the challenger must break the chain, not pick at isolated verses. Each reply below puts the challenger's term back in its chain.

## 0. The pincer from the challenger's own grants

1. The challenger grants that Mary was a virgin when the angel spoke. [L1 Luke 1:27, 34, as granted]
2. The challenger reads Matthew 1:25, "knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son", as abstinence running to the birth. [L1 Matthew 1:25, as read by the challenger]
3. The conception is future at Luke 1:31, "thou shalt conceive in thy womb", and is past at Matthew 1:18, "found with child". It falls between those two points. [L1]

So there is no moment in which Joseph "knew Mary his wife within the espousal" before the conception. The challenger's keystone, "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal", is contradicted by the challenger's own reading of "till". [L4, resting on Luke 1:31-34 and Matthew 1:18, 25]

## 1. The "husband" rows (against D1)

[L1] Matthew 1:19 says "Joseph her husband" and Matthew 1:18 says "before they came together". The title is therefore used while the text says there was no union. In this chapter, "husband" is a legal title and carries no seed. [L3] Deuteronomy 22:23-24 treats a betrothed woman as "his neighbour's wife" before union.

[L1] Matthew 1:19: Joseph was "minded to put her away privily". If Joseph were the father, nothing would have troubled him. The angel does not answer, "the child is yours." He answers, "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost" (1:20). [L4, resting on Matthew 1:19-20 and Deuteronomy 22:23-24]

[L2] Matthew 1:2-16 has thirty-nine "begat" verbs (ἐγέννησεν, egennēsen, "begat"), running to "Jacob begat Joseph". There is no fortieth, "Joseph begat Jesus". The text changes to ἐξ ἧς ἐγεννήθη (ex hēs egennēthē, "out of whom was born"). The challenger grants the morphology. The challenger says a verse that stops short of naming the father is not a verse that denies him. The verse does not stand alone. Verses 18-20 supply the source, "of the Holy Ghost."

## 2. "Of the Holy Ghost" (against D2)

- [L2] Matthew himself uses ἐκ (ek, "out of") for the mother as source of a begotten child: "Judas begat Phares and Zara of Thamar" (1:3), also verses 5-6. In 1:20 the thing conceived, γεννηθὲν (gennēthen, "that which is begotten"), is ἐν αὐτῇ (en autē, "in her"), and its ek is the Spirit. The setting is a physical womb, not a spiritual new birth.
- [L1, L3] John 1:13 shows how the text speaks when it excludes human paternity: "not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man." The challenger cites John 1:13 for believers. Matthew 1:18-20 states the literal case.
- [L1] The challenger says no κατὰ σάρκα (kata sarka, "according to flesh") is attached to Matthew 1:20. Romans 1:3 uses kata sarka for descent from David, not for the conception. That marker is not needed at 1:20, because "found with child" is already physical.
- [L2] The challenger says ἐπελεύσεται (epeleusetai, "will come upon") and ἐπισκιάσει (episkiasei, "will overshadow") mean anointing and presence. The verbs need not denote begetting. The question at Luke 1:34 is how conception happens, and the answer at 1:35 names the Holy Ghost and no man. Luke 1:37, "with God nothing shall be impossible", marks a sign, as does Genesis 18:14. [L3, resting on Luke 1:34-37 and Genesis 18:14]
- [L1] "Called" and "therefore". Luke 1:35 gives the reason: "Therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee." The challenger's parallel, 1 Chronicles 28:6, says "I have chosen him to be my son" about a son David begat. It says nothing of a "therefore" caused by the Holy Ghost's coming.
- [L1, L3] The naming does not make Joseph the biological father. The angel also told Mary, "thou shalt call his name JESUS" (Luke 1:31). Eve named Seth (Genesis 4:25). Mordecai "took" Esther "for his own daughter" (Esther 2:7), so a legal act establishes the relation without seed.

## 3. The timing rows (against D3)

On Luke 1:34, "Noted. Not conceding here. Goes to review." The present tense of γινώσκω (ginōskō, "I know") is not the point. The question looks forward to a future conception, "how shall this be", given her present state. Joseph is already her betrothed, so if marriage were the answer there would be no question. The angel answers with the Holy Ghost, not with Joseph. I claim no vow.

[L1] Matthew 1:18's συνέρχομαι (synerchomai, "come together") is dated by 1:25. Joseph "knew her not" until the birth. The challenger's "till" reading of 1:25 cuts against his own keystone (see section 0).

Brothers and sisters (Mark 6:3) concern later children, not the conception. Nothing in my chain depends on perpetual virginity.

[L1, L2] Isaiah 7:14 is a sign. Isaiah 7:11 says, "ask thee a sign... in the depth, or in the height above." The Hebrew is אוֹת (ʼôth, "sign"). A young woman's ordinary pregnancy is no sign. [L3] Joel 1:8 shows that בְּתוּלָה (bethulah, "virgin") can be used of a wife bewailing "the husband of her youth." So the Hebrew word the challenger prefers is not clearer. Genesis 24:16 and 24:43 apply both words to Rebekah. [L1] The KJV margin the challenger cites reads "virgin". Matthew 1:23 says παρθένος (parthenos, "virgin").

## 4. "Thy father" (against D4)

- [L1] Luke 2:48-49: Mary says "thy father", and the child answers in the next breath, "my Father's business." Verse 50: "they understood not the saying." The contrast is in the text.
- [L1] The same narrator who wrote "parents" also wrote Luke 3:23, "(as was supposed)", and Luke 1:34-35. A narrator cannot be set against himself. In Luke's own narration (2:33, 43), the text says "Joseph and his mother", not "his father". The only "thy father" is Mary's, and Jesus' reply is the next verse.
